utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we invite the witness to come in and -- I think he can be escorted in already. I briefly deal with a matter which is the statement of Dragisa Masal. On the 18th of March, the Defence brought to the attention of the Chamber that the English translation of D942, and that is the witness statement of Dragisa Masal, seemed to include text which could not be found in the original B/C/S version; specifically, the first sentence of paragraph 11. You can find this on transcript page 33330 up to -332. On the 19th of March, CLSS clarified that the English text uploaded under D942 corresponds with the B/C/S text that CLSS received for translation but that the B/C/S text of D942 is, however, not the same as originally submitted to CLSS by the Defence. And the Chamber invites the Defence to give its comments on this very unfortunate way of proceeding today. As a matter of fact, by the end of the first session, because the witness is, first of all, he is coming into the courtroom, but, of course, we'll then conclude hearing the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you want me to respond now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if can you do that. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I can. I think in the chronology what's missing is that the English translation that was uploaded we advised in the proofing statement that there was a paragraph missing from paragraph number, I believe, it's 23 or 27 a subparagraph that was not in the English translation. Then I was advised that we had this translation that apparently had been made from the draft unsigned statement that had been presented to CLSS, and I submitted it, and then on the day of the witness starting is when the Prosecution and I talked and it was brought to my attention that the extra two sentences, or however it is, in paragraph 11 exist. So that is the chronology. There were two separate translations made. Both are at the -- both have been -- are available in the sense that the Prosecution had -- has both translations. The issue as to other minor differences, I don't even know what they are since CLSS has not specified them, so I was going to send the signed original, which the witness has now attested, to CLSS to have them prepare a final English translation that is adequately reflecting what is in the signed B/C/S original. And that is how the Defence would -- what the Defence would have to say on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the Chamber would have appreciated this whole chronology, to learn about it, prior to being confronted with the fact that there are differences between the original and the English translation. Mr. Weber, you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Originally we had just opposed paragraph 11 and it was marked for identification, but actually if the Prosecution could still reserve its position related to the other differences that might be in there. Right now it's not very clear to us either what it might be, and I just wanted to put that on the record. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It should have been clarified in the detail given today rather than to suggest. Because when I asked specifically how could this have possibly happened, because that's what I did, I think I even used the words "did they invent part of the text," the explanation as given today was not given at that time but apparently the information was available to the Defence. I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Masal, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, but I'll first remind the witness that you're still bound by, Mr. Masal, you're still bound by the declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, we left off last week talking about the part of the cross-examination focusing on convoys which were not reaching Zepa and the food shortages caused thereby.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 65 ter number 25880 in e-court. While we wait for the document, I can say it's an intelligence report from the organ for security and intelligence of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade dated 31 December 1993, and I'd like to take a look at the bottom of the page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the English it's approximately the fourth line from the bottom and is in relation to Zepa and says: "People live well because there's enough food. The reserves of flour and other articles of food are enormous. Some people have as much as 50 kilograms of flour or even more. Very large quantities of food, medicines and other medical supplies are under the control of the army." Sir, is this information consistent with the type of information that you had about what was going on in Zepa with regard to the food and medicine?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I received such reports from subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was your understanding or information about what the BiH army was doing with the food and medicine that it had under its control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of our information surplus food, or rather food that was "preserved" by powerful people from the military or the civilian area, these surpluses were transferred between enclaves, and these products were resold at exorbitant prices. To put it very briefly: Consumer goods were smuggled as was food, alcohol, and cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document as the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That makes Exhibit D957, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D957 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would next like to take a look at P7229, which was used on Thursday by the Prosecution, and at transcript page 33374. And once that comes up, I'd like to look at page 2 in the English and the bottom of the first page in the Serbian. That again is a document from the BiH Supreme Command in Sarajevo. And the -- in the -- in the B/C/S, it's the very last two lines on the first page. In English, it's the last paragraph before the heading: "2nd Corps Zone of Responsibility." And it's talking about OG Gorazde's zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it says as follows: "Despite tough enemy attacks and threats our forces are sturdily holding all defence lines and successfully repelling all the Chetnik attacks." What was your understanding of where the ABiH had placed their defence lines in relation to the town of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the date of this information, if you mean this period it is the 12th of February, 1993. At that time, the positions were very close to Visegrad. The hydroelectric power plant Visegrad was being fired at. The town of Visegrad was within the range of mortars of smallest calibre, so in this period - in this period - the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were just before Visegrad, Rogatica, and Rudo. Rudo, say, about 15 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did that change in the time-period following the 12th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely for these reasons. For these reasons: The Army of Republika Srpska, or rather the Tactical Group Visegrad, planned combat activities in order to repel the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that they would be outside the range of Visegrad, Rogatica, and Rudo, so in that operation the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were repelled all the way back to Ustipraca; that is to say, 12 kilometres away from Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can move to P7231, which was used in cross at transcript page 33377 and onwards. When we see that document, we'll see it's dated the 14th --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but just maybe so we can move first efficiently, can we just have a little context for when that was? The last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, the last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what time-period it was where the -- the ABiH moved to 12 kilometres away from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Operation Mac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We know when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at this document from the -- this is again a document from the BiH side. Looking at page 2 in both languages, it is at the top of the page in the Serbian and in the middle of the page in English. It's the first bullet point under: "Requests." And it says here: "OG IB Gorazde requests that the VK staff's order" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "OG IB Gorazde requests that the VK staff's order that all persons liable for military service from Zenica, Jablanica, and Konjic return to its zone of responsibility be respected." We know that OB [sic] refers to "operative group," as is identified on the first page of this document. What was your understanding or information about the size or strength of this operative group of the BiH army, the OG IB Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you explain "OB." What is "OG" and "IB"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant to say "OG" because that's the -- well, ... on page 1, we have "IB" being "Eastern Bosnia" in the English, and we have "OG" as "operations group." Those are the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So could you tell me, sir, what was your information about the strength or size of the operative group of the BiH army, OG IB Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the assessments made in my command, or rather the reports of the intelligence organs, Operations Group Gorazde had about six brigades. They had about 15.000 men, about three times more than the units of the Tactical Group Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what kind of locations did the Operative Group Gorazde use to base its troops and equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the operations group was in Gorazde. The command of a few brigades - I don't know exactly which ones - was also in Gorazde. Then one command was in the village of Osanica; that is, towards Foca. And there was one command to the north of the town of Gorazde in the area of the Pobjeda factory. The units or rather the defence areas or the areas of operations of brigades were towards the units, or rather brigades, of Tactical Group Visegrad; that is to say, towards Rudo, Cajnice, Visegrad, Rogatica, and towards Foca. However, Operations Group Gorazde of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had quite a reserve, and they were in the areas in the broader region of Gorazde, and they were prepared to take action along certain axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify, sir, in talking about the broader region of Gorazde, are you talking about the enclave of Gorazde or the town of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the town of Gorazde. That is to say, Gorazde, along with its outskirts, the suburban neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now taking as a reference in time when Gorazde was declared a safe area, how did the size and strength of the ABiH forces in Gorazde town compare both before and after the declaration of Gorazde as a safe area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the strength of the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not change drastically, if the period before the safe area was declared is compared to the one after that. However, Gorazde had open communication with Sarajevo, and that road was used for bringing in fresh forces, for returning deserters, as we saw from those documents, and for the intervention of the units of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now in relation to the situation in Gorazde, you testified at transcript page 33422 that the Operation Zvijezda 94 was intended to return Serb residents to their villages in Gorazde. Can you tell us when and why they had left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms. From when the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs in Gorazde held about half of the territory -- or rather, almost half of the territory was populated, and the Army of Republika Srpska held a bit more than half the territory. At any rate, the VRS had under its control the right bank of the Drina river, then the suburban neighbourhoods to the north, towards Rogatica, and partly towards Cajnice up to the Kozara pass. The rest was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sometime toward the end of 1992, all the Serbs of Gorazde were expelled from the right bank of the Drina river where they had been the majority population. Then also from the neighbourhood of Obarak that is on the outskirts towards Ustipraca, and it's between the village of Kopaci, the current seat of the Serbian municipality of Gorazde, and another municipality where there is a -- an Orthodox church and an Orthodox cemetery. Then Jabuka and Jabucko Sedlo. All of these villages were Serb villages that practically towards the end of 1992, as the Serbs were expelled from the territory of Gorazde, were destroyed and torched. And -- sorry, just one more thing. Two Serb villages with about 50 families remained underneath Grebak - that is to say, between Grebak and Jabucko Sedlo - they were under constant blockade and they were not allowed -- even when operation Zvijezda 94 was over, they were not allowed to move out. I mean, those who had survived. They were not allowed to move out of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at 1D00588. Pardon me, 558. 1D558.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we look at that, could I ask the witness a question. Witness, you said that the Operations Group Gorazde had about six brigades, 15.000 men. We looked at a document in which it was said that the order that persons returned from -- return to the zone of responsibility of the Operations Group Gorazde coming from Zenica, Jablanica, and Konjic should be respected. Now those 15.000, are those inclusive those who were still to return, or were these reserve? You said there was considerable reserve. Could you explain a little bit how the 15.000 came to your mind when looking at a document which says that people still have to return to the zone of responsibility of the operation group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that this is a smaller group. It's not a big number of military conscripts whose families went out into the area of Zenica, Konjic, and Jablanica. And afterwards they were supposed to return to their units, so I do not consider that number to be significant as compared to these 15.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But are they part of the 15.000 or are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, according to our estimate it was always around 15.000. I think that that number was included as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that it was a smaller number, you said, that's what you assumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've lost the document. If we can have again 1D558 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a publication of the US house of representatives republican research committee in the task force on terrorism and conventional warfare from May 4th, 1994. It's in English, so I'll have to read for you the section I want to first focus you on, which is the last half of the first paragraph and the first five lines of the second paragraph. "However, while Bosnian Serb aggressiveness has undoubtedly played a large part in the Gorazde tragedy, what is less known is the role played by the Bosnian government and military in instigating the conflict and in efforts to draw the West, particularly the United States, into the war generally. "The roots of this situation derive from the events of the fall of 1992 at a relatively early stage of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, the Gorazde area was one of the first places where Islamist guerrillas, a combined force of Afghan volunteers (mainly Arab Afghans) and Bosnian Islamists, had embarked on a systematic campaign against the local Christian population in order to secure a predominant military position." Is this accurately describing, sir, the situation in the fall of 1992 according to your information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been read into the record now, but just in terms of carrying on like this, we would object eventually here. It's leading. It's presenting information to the witness instead of eliciting it from him, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we're talking about what to do in the future. Not what you did until now. Any comments on what Mr. Weber has drawn our attention to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, and we have -- the witness has given his testimony about the end of 1992, and I am presenting a document prepared by some other people to see if this is what he was talking about, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually the scope of the examination I believe largely related, and I'm not sure even I talked about his duties during 1992 except to ask him his position, but his time in TG Visegrad picked up at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, please be very precise on the matter in the future, Mr. Ivetic. Certainly the portion you read goes beyond what the witness was examined on until now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer the question, sir, or do you need my ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My previous answer about the expulsion of the Serbs from the territory of Gorazde is corroborated by this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What information did the VRS have as to the efforts or desire of the BiH authorities in Gorazde to obtain the military intervention of the west or the United States?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything specific about this particular period. I only know that the offensives of the BiH army towards the end of 1992 were large scale. Within the scope of three or four days, the Serbian population was expelled from the general area of Gorazde. After that, when Gorazde was proclaimed a protected area, the BiH army continued intense preparation to expand its territory and to have control over the entire area of Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness moved well away from your question. Could you please next time stop him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to be very precise in your answer, sir, and tell us about any information that you -- that you or the VRS had about the BiH side's efforts to obtain military intervention on their behalf once Gorazde had been declared a safe area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what I was going to say. Active sabotage activities and then preparations for offensives and offensives on particular axes, especially towards Cajnice, all that was aimed to provoke the Army of Republika Srpska at all costs. As a result, the VRS would be exposed to threats; i.e., the threats that it would be bombed by NATO air force would come to fruition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, for Your Honours' reference, page 5 of this document in the last half talks about precisely that attempt at provoking the Republika Srpska for threats of bombings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you also about the reporting in the media in relation to Gorazde. Did you have occasion to learn of any media reporting that misrepresented the situation in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to inform both you and the Trial Chamber that when Operation Zvijezda 94 was being planned, the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, who was the chief of the General Staff, and the commander of the Herzegovina Corps, General Grubac, explicitly put a ban on fire being opened on the Gorazde sector before fighting started in the town of Gorazde itself. However, from the very outset of the operation, Radio Gorazde and the other media of Bosnia-Herzegovina reported daily about hundreds and thousands of dead and wounded in Gorazde, and especially in those parts and institutions that should have been protected from any combat activities. I'm repeating: There was a ban on artillery fire on Gorazde up until the beginning of fighting on the ground at the very entrance to Gorazde. However, we have already seen what kind of reports were sent to the world about hundreds and thousands of dead and wounded. It was all propaganda. When all of that ended, one could easily see what was the truth when they entered Gorazde itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we could turn to page 10 of this document. It's the last paragraph on page 10 and goes on to page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is it your understanding that "we have already seen" includes the Chamber? Now, the witness says: "However, we have already seen what kind of reports were sent to the world," and of course in order to fully understand and appreciate that, I wondered whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think we had approximately three newspaper articles that were presented by the Prosecution in cross-examination. I'm not sure if that's what the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's what the witness referred to. What did you refer to exactly, Witness, when you said: "... we have already what kind of seen reports were sent to the world about hundreds and thousands of dead and wounded," and that it was all propaganda? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is about what the Prosecutor showed us, a report from Los Angeles Post, a report heard on Radio Gorazde, and the report by monitors who compiled their reports based on that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The monitors are part of the media in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced because at the time the monitors did not move anywhere from Gorazde. They relied on the BiH army and the command of the OG and Radio Gorazde for their information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not exactly an answer to my question, but I do understand the context you are giving us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I will read this section to you and ask for your comments based upon your knowledge of what was going on at the time about what is being reported here. "That said, it was now possible to objectively assess the actual situation in Gorazde. It soon became clear that the Bosnian Muslims had overstated the plight of the city. The casualty levels were far below initial reports, with UNHCR, the most responsible among those reporting sources, having initially alleged that there were 715 killed and 1970 wounded, over 600 of them serious and requiring evacuations by air. Most of these casualties, the UNHCR had stressed, were innocent civilians. However, post-action inspection revealed that there were some 200 fatalities and some 200 seriously wounded, 70 per cent of them Muslim soldiers." And let's for the moment stop there, and I'll ask for your comment as to what is written here, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This tallies with what I have said and it also confirms what I said, and that was that from the beginning of Operation Zvijezda 94, there was a ban on opening artillery fire on the general sector of Gorazde. Therefore, after an inspection, it was established that most of the casualties came from the ranks of the BiH army and that they were killed on the front line as they were fighting the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned radio reports. I'd like to read the next sentence in this report: "The extent of the damage to the hospital and other buildings, not to speak of Gorazde overall, was far below what had been anticipated on the basis of radio reports. Indeed, on 28 April, General Rose went on an inspection tour of the Gorazde enclave. He returned full of criticism of the Bosnian Muslims, adding that they had exaggerated the number of wounded and the damage done to the town in the Bosnian Serb offensive in order to instigate NATO's military intervention." The -- I'd ask for your comment on this part of the report, especially as to damage to structures.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report by General Rose completely refutes what was portrayed through propaganda. I personally met with General Rose in my command in Kopaci when he paid us a visit. For about half an hour, we analysed the treatment of UNPROFOR in Gorazde, a cease-fire, and General Rose presented several facts which confirmed that the attitude of the VRS towards UNPROFOR and its activities were positive. He did not proffer any comments on the number of casualties. I suppose that he wanted to keep that to himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is there any documentary source for General Rose's observations which is either in evidence or could be produced as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have this report, and then we have a report from Mr. Yasushi Akashi commenting on this report and saying that it's generally report. I don't know if that's what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On this report, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it heavily relies on post-action inspection and what General Rose said, and I would expect under those circumstances that there must be a report by General Rose or that it ... Is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do know that there is also an interview from French TV 1, which is cited in paragraph 5 that I mentioned earlier, but I have not been able to go through all the documents that have been disclosed to us to find out if we have a report from General Rose. Like I said, I do have a report from Mr. Yasushi Akashi to Kofi Annan talking about this report, the one that we've been looking at now from the research committee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the next document I was going to discuss with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Weber, if you would aware of any Rose report which could shed further light on it, we would have then even the more direct evidence on what is claimed here as the position of General Rose. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could look at -- pardon me. Do you have any additional information to provide as to the hospital in Gorazde and reports of damage to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't have any information. I learnt about all that during the Prosecutor's examination. Apart from that, I didn't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will move on to 1D2939, which is the 12 July 1994 report of Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I meanwhile ask, Witness, where this report says, "However, post-action inspection...," and then a few lines down: "General Rose went on an inspection tour of the Gorazde enclave," did you mean with post-action inspection that inspection tour by General Rose or was there any post-action inspection performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that General Rose was there. I don't know who else was with him. After the end of the operation, I'm sure that you know that, one UNPROFOR battalion, an English battalion and a Ukrainian battalion, entered Gorazde and took positions on the left and the right banks, the English and the Ukrainian, battalions respectively. After that, UNPROFOR convoys arrived, as well as UN observers, and I suppose that they carried out inspections and sent reports. I had announcements of their arrivals, but I didn't know what their mission was. I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in this document from Akashi to Annan, in the first paragraph, it says: "As requested at your fax of 25 June 1994, we have reviewed the US house republican research committee report of 4 May 1994 on Gorazde. We find the paper lacks objectivity." Then if we go to the third paragraph, it says: "Our records indicate that operations around Gorazde after 20 March 1994 generally unfolded as outlined in the report. However, we do not agree with the congressional report's overall assessment and interpretation of the crisis as a one-sided attempt by the Bosnians to provoke the Serbs and to draw the outside world into the conflict. As outlined in the report of SG pursuant to SCR 844 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down, Mr. Ivetic, while reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... SCR 844, 1993, the Bosnians did conduct some military activities from within the pocket. They also expressed to the SR SG and commander BH command their expectation of much greater use of NATO air support once the town was attacked. However, Serb behaviour during and after the offensive makes it clear that retention of the areas captured, including the right bank opposite the town of Gorazde, is one of their objectives." So we're talking about the report we just looked at, and I'd like to look at the specific complaints of Mr. Akashi of either incorrect or different information that is on page 2, and I'd like to get your comment about the factual scenario, whether it's supports what is being written here. And if we could look at page 2 and the second paragraph, Mr. Akashi writes: "Allegations that UNHCR convoys moved military materials into Gorazde are totally unfounded and are reminiscent of far-fetched Serb propaganda. The Serbs have always been particularly zealous in their searching of UNHCR convoys bounds for Gorazde and have on repeated occasions removed items such as shoes or sleeping bags on the ground they constitute military material." What factual information can you provide for us, sir, on this topic, the movement the military materials into Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large majority of the UNHCR convoys were okay; i.e., the contents of the convoys were in keeping with the declaration. However, I can say for a fact that in certain vehicles of certain convoys the originally pre-packed packages of food were replaced by certain quantities of ammunition. It was not a -- done on a large-scale, but on several occasions ammunition was found. After that, there was a detailed inspection of every convoy. Convoys which did not contain such packages would be inspected very quickly and allowed to go on. Wherever there was a doubt that there was something suspicious in the convoy, there was a quick check and then a detailed inspection of the convoy. There were not many such cases. I claim that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can then direct your attention to the next paragraph, which I will have to read for you to get a translation, quote: "For those periods when our observers were able to patrol, we are certain that the hospital was not used for military purposes. There was at least one artillery piece near the Red Cross building, but this did not represent a particular concentration of BiH weaponry within the small area of Gorazde that remained under Bosnian control in the final stages of the battle. UNMO [sic] also confirmed that no BiH used their building. At least two mortars were beside the building, and their vehicles were stolen for use by the BiH." Do you have any information as to the use of the hospital, the grouping of artillery near the Red Cross building, or the use of the region -- the area by the UNMO base by the BiH?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the initial stages of the operation, we did not have that conformation. However, as the operation was drawing to an end, the town could be fully observed by our forces from our positions on the elevations around the town. We had full visual control of the entire town, and we could observe every activity and every action in every part of the town. So it is completely correct that in the vicinity of certain institutions and facilities, there were artillery positions or deployment sectors of certain logistics elements. I personally was not familiar with the town of Gorazde. However, a lot of the officers from the Gorazde Brigade and a lot of the troops were very familiar with the town, and they knew very well in which part of the town the fire -- fire was opened by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as well as 1D00558, the republican research committee report that is being commented upon in this Akashi fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection to either document pending a completion of the translation. But just so we have it on the record, the Prosecution would note for the record that the last paragraph of the document before us, 1D2939, appears to refer to P7243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D558 will be MFI D958, Your Honours. And 65 ter 1D2939 will be MFI D959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D958 and D959 are marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we would additionally from the bar table seek to admit 65 ter number 18766, dated 13 April 1994, from Mr. Akashi, and it's a discussion as to ABiH provocations and military actions, so the Chamber can have the full breadth of the factual scenario from that time-period before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could just take a quick look at that over the recess and any related material and then I could come back right after the recess with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, I tried to avoid the word "bar table" recently because what we are talking about is documentary evidence which relates to portions of the testimony of a witness but which are not introduced through that witness. That's the kind of construction you are -- you want to be applied, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. You've been much more explicit than I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No -- then we'll hear from Mr. Weber after the break. But could we already reserve a number for it, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D960, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved. We'll hear from Mr. Weber after the break. Are you -- apart from that, are you done, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have more to go through. Approximately 35 minutes. But these documents sometimes take some time since we have to read them to the witness, but I hope to go faster after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break first, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00. You may follow the usher, Mr. Masal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber you would come back to us after the break and that's now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With respect to 65 ter 18766, the Prosecution has no objection with that being admitted from the bar table. We did have an opportunity to speak to the Defence about related materials. At this time, the Prosecution would also tender 65 ter 09614. We would be tendering that as a P exhibit, and we would note for the record that there is also related information in admitted Exhibit P586. So provided the additional Prosecution exhibit is admitted, we no objection to the other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you avoid the word "bar table," then have better chances of success with Mr. Ivetic not objecting. But, Mr. Ivetic, could you already express yourself on the document now tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can, Your Honours. As Mr. Weber has said, we have talked about this and we are on agreement on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then 65 ter 18766 had received -- a number was reserved already, that's D960, is hereby admitted. And 65 ter 09614 receives what P number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7249 is admitted into ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I almost said evidence. Mr. Weber, there seems to be no B/C/S translation for it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see we do have one. I don't know if it's been released. We will release it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there were no objections, may I take it that the B/C/S -- the release -- if it is not released within the next hour, Mr. Ivetic, you have 24 hours to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then now I complete my sentence: P7249 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have been informed that it's been released, the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I'd like to move to some VRS documents. If we could turn to 65 ter number 00138. While we wait for that, you'll see it's dated 16 April 1994 and is from General Ratko Mladic. Now, sir, looking at the recipients of this document, are you one of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now looking at the text beginning at item number 1: "I most strictly forbid inhumane treatment, ill-treatment, and physical liquidation of the civilian population, prisoners of war, and members of international organisations." "2, All commands and members of the VRS are duty-bound to isolate and protect the civilian population of Gorazde by way of moving them to suitable locations," and onward. Is this stance of General Mladic as to how the VRS was to act in Goradze, how did it compare with your knowledge of his overall stance of how the VRS was supposed to act in regards to other battle zones?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that during this operation, although propaganda said this, we did not have an opportunity to come across destroyed villages and massive liquidations of civilians. We did not have an opportunity to come across villages where there were civilians left, so we realised that civilians had left the settlements before the members of the military did. As for the other areas of responsibility, again, I can say -- well, not with certainty, because I wasn't there myself, but I do know that the general position was that the civilian population should not be exposed to combat operations to the highest degree possible, should not be imperiled in any way. I'll give one example, if allow me. In the previous operation, the entire population of the villages of Kosanica and Medjedja that were blocked because the road near Ustipraca was cut off, agreement was reached through radio communication between the commander of one combat group that was within my units and the commander of the opposite side - this was a gentlemanly thing do, it was a militarily responsible thing to do - to allow everyone safe passage to Gorazde and that has already been shown before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we decide on that, Witness, the stamp at the bottom, do you know what kind of a stamp, what -- what does it indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The square stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's not a classical stamp. This square stamp is the stamp of the command that received this telegram. We say that that is in the office where all documents that arrive are registered. Whatever is received as a telegram or through teleprinters or ... I mean, I cannot read this out very well. It says: Command of the 1st, maybe Podrinje, Light Brigade. And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is this a stamp which confirms receipt of the document by the owner of the stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as why the stamp says 31st of December, 1995, where the document apparently dates from the 16th of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't. Maybe there was no stamp in the first place and then when it was being archived it was stamped subsequently, but I really have no real explanation as to why this is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we can all assume many things about it. Mr. Ivetic, do you have any -- any further comment on, I would say, on my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. It's a Prosecution document. That's how we received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weber, do you have any explanation as to where it comes from and is there any explanation for this date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In terms of the date, no. The document reflects what we know about the information. In terms of the -- where it comes from, I'm just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Of course, everyone can assume or imagine that it's the date of filing or whatever. But that's the reason why I asked the witness what kind of a stamp this is. Now, the text of the stamp apparently doesn't say anything about received, et cetera, but I leave it to that for the time being. You have no objections, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. You asked the questions about what I was curious about. And with respect to just further information, it does from the Drina Corps collection, so this could be from archived material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D961, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D961 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to now look at 65 ter number 00132.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, General, you'll see it's dated 22 April, 1994, and also from General Mladic. Looking at the recipients of this -- well, first of all, looking at this order, is this an order that was received by you in relation to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it says here: "As there is still sporadic artillery-mortar fire being sent into the city of Gorazde despite the issued order, in order to consistently comply with the order of the president of the RS, I hereby order: ... I most strictly forbid artillery, mortar and PA fire being sent into the part of the city of Gorazde on the left bank of the Drina river." Now, do you recall if during this time-period there was an issue with some units still shooting into the town? What was going on that would cause them to still shoot into the town of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. Compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please split it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if there was an issue with some units still shooting into the town during the time-period of this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was individual firing in the area of Gorazde. There was this looming danger; namely, if this were to continue, that the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska would be bombed by NATO and the already agreed upon cease-fires could be done away with, and that is why this order was sent to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was there anything going on that would explain or cause why -- explain why this [indiscernible] units were firing into the town?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were provocations from the other side. There was mortar fire and also there was fire in immediate combat contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D962, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D962 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we put the 65 ter number on the record again because it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 65 ter number should be number 00132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now turn to 65 ter number 09749.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask -- was there no problem in relation to the right bank of the Drina river in Gorazde? It limits itself to the left bank, this order? Was there any relevant difference between the left bank and the right bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously there were these provocations on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any difference in population between the right bank and the left bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no difference in the population. The Serb population hadn't returned yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was the Serb population which had left, had they been living mainly on the left bank or mainly on the right bank or equally divided over the two banks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In town, they were mostly on the right bank, but in the suburban neighbourhoods on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 9749.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is dated 7 September 1993, and is typed-signed Dragisa Masal. First of all, sir, looking at this document, is this an authentic order of yours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we see here also you order to cease all artillery attacks on the town of Gorazde, and you say: "In case of enemy attack, a counterattack is to be launched with the approval of the superior command but only against spotted targeted in contact and against firing positions behind the enemy artillery." Is this consistent with the orders that you received from the superior command or is this of your own initiative? Could you tell us how this came about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, orders arrived from the superior command as well. However, I issued this order because a few times from the command of the Drina Corps, orders were received not to do anything unnecessary or irresponsible that would disrupt the already fragile cease-fire agreement that had been reached. This is solely for the purpose of keeping the cease-fire, maintaining it, and also ensuring conditions for lasting peace in the territory concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could tender this document Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D963, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we now turn to P731.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This was a document that was shown to you during the cross-examination at transcript page 33429. While we wait for that, it is from the TG Visegrad signed by you and dated the 11th of April, 1994. And you were asked about item number 7 on this document, and you were asked if you indeed conveyed the message from General Mladic. Now I want to ask you a different question. As a professional army officer, how did you understand General Mladic's message here; for instance, who are the Turks he is talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one sentence before this answer. I have already said that in 1992 the entire Serb population had been expelled from the area of Gorazde. Here, specifically, I conveyed the message of General Mladic as I understood it and as we understood it, generally. Turks were the soldiers of the opposite side, not with the intention of portraying them as Turks, really. I mean, they called us aggressors, they called us Chetniks, we called them Turks or something along those lines, and it exclusively pertained to soldiers of the other side. At least that is how I understood it and how I interpreted it to my subordinates, officers and soldiers. As for this area, my understanding was the area where I was; that is to say, the area of Gorazde, or rather the area that was supposed to be liberated so that the Serb population could come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now General Mladic is reported as saying: "Pay no attention to what is going on around us." What was going on around you at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO air strikes and the threat of a full escalation of bombing in Serb-held areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now you were asked about -- I'd like to move from Gorazde and move to a different topic. You were asked quite a few questions about Strpci. I want to look at P7235, which you were shown. This is a letter from the collegium of the railway line that was discussed with you at transcript page 33399. And at that time, you said that none of the authorities mentioned in the letter - that is to say, the MUP of Serbia, the assistant defence minister of Serbia, or the state security police of Serbia - ever informed you about the contents of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I see we're still waiting for it to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, sir, when was the first time that you saw this document or heard that someone claimed that the Serbian army was planning an abduction of civilians from a train?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you ever receive or know of any orders from within the VRS planning for such an abduction of Muslim civilians from a train?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered in part when giving answers to the Prosecutor. As for this event, the Army of Republika Srpska not at a single point in time thought about it or planned it. As for this event, I was informed about it when it actually happened. Since this had to do with a kidnapping of civilians, the military organisation did not take measures because it was the civilian structures that were supposed to investigate and continue proceedings. My command, the military structure, did not deal with this. Finally just one detail. The command of the tactical group is a temporary command and its sole task is to organise and carry out combat operations in a particular zone and in a certain period of time. As for civilian affairs and the obligations of the civilian authorities, the command could not have dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could turn to P7237, which was also shown to you in connection with this set of facts. Now, sir, I know that the B/C/S is hard to read. Hopefully you can focus on that. Now, this was -- this presents as a -- or purports to be from the Drina Corps command and from the OB department, intelligence and security of the same. I want you to focus at the person that is alleged to be signing this document, and I want to ask you: Are you familiar with Jovo Maric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo Maric was a general, the chief of the air force and aircraft defences in the Main Staff. Who this is, I have no idea whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What happened to the Jovo Maric that you know, that you've just described as a general and chief of the air force and aircraft defences in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of the air force and air defence, General Jovo Maric, he was a pilot, and towards the very end of the war, or rather at the end of the war, unfortunately, he lost his life in a traffic accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was General Jovo Maric ever fulfilling duties within the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he was not carrying out duties there. That I know. All the time he was on the Main Staff. He was chief of the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know when he attained the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that when I came to the Main Staff in 1994 Jovo Maric was a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a Colonel Jovo Maric working in the intelligence and security department of the Drina Corps during the time-period when you were subordinated to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew Vujadin Popovic who was head of the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to turn some matters that are contained in the document itself. First of all, it says here that a military vehicle of the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade was "forcibly seized" in Visegrad, which was driven by Uros Pljevacevic. Sir, did you order anyone to forcibly seize a military vehicle from your own subordinated brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Dragan Sekaric is listed here as one of those who seized the vehicle. Have you ever heard of Dragan Sekaric; that is to say, was he ever a member of the VRS units subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name doesn't ring a bell. Obviously he was a foot soldier, and I really didn't know the names of the soldiers in subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Boban Indjic is listed here, and you did say that he was a member of the Intervention Platoon within the Visegrad Brigade. Did he ever receive orders either from you or from the VRS Main Staff to forcibly take a military vehicle to be used in the abduction of civilians from a train at Strpci?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct you. Boban Indjic was the commander of the intervention company, not just one platoon in the intervention company. He did not receive any combat orders from me. He could only receive combat orders from his brigade commander. I don't know. I'm not aware of any of his superiors ever having issued such an order to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I would next like to look at 65 ter number 32206. And I'd ask you to take look at the Serbian version very carefully and let me know if, in fact, this is an authentic document authored by you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a telegram. Clearly the signature is mine -- or rather, in the heading, we can read Visegrad TG.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd ask you to carefully look at the beginning of the document and see whether you recall that this is something that you authored or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the brigade commander worked in his area and what he did was based on what he thought he should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recognise this document as one authored by you; that is to say, is this an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that in my oral report, I submitted the same contents as found in this report to General Zivanovic. So it's about the same thing. I don't know whether the same message was also conveyed in a written form, perhaps through the communications centre. I don't know. I am only aware of the fact I remember that I sought assistance because I did not have a security organ in my unit. I sought assistance from the military police to curb certain negative phenomenon in the zone of responsibility of the brigade; i.e., tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could tender this as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D964, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at transcript page 33416, in response to a question from Judge Fluegge, you indicated that Milan Lukic, who was mentioned in one of the last documents or the prior -- the one prior to this one, was not within your units of and was not subordinated to you in any other way. Could you please elaborate for us on how it was that this individual was not subordinated to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean he -- that he was not subordinated to the brigade, he was not -- it was not possible for him to be subordinated to the tactical group. Only officers and non-commissioned officers could be subordinated to the tactical group. A small number of them. In the area of the 2nd Brigade around Visegrad as well as in the territories of some other unit, not only the 2nd Brigade, there were members who were not members of the brigade. They were not military conscripts. In other words, they acted of their own will. They had their own goals, ambitions, and objectives. To cut a long story short, there was a fear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in the future, if we could have actually what was asked, because I do not see Judge Fluegge actually asking that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look. Against my habit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At least no question in relation to Milan Lukic. That was a question by the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that makes the question any less important, but leave to that. Let me just have a look whether the question is the same because it may not be that relevant. Yes, I think the question, irrespective of who did put the question ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could move onto P7236, this was again showed to you at transcript page 33400, and your answer at that time -- let's wait for the document. This is in relation to the information from your subordinate units about Sandzak Muslims, and your answer at that time was: "I did order but I did not order them to capture civilians but rather Muslims who often travelled from Sandzak through my zone of responsibility in the direction of Gorazde and Sarajevo. This has nothing to do with civilians." Could you please explain for us what these Muslims from Sandzak were doing as they travelled through your zone of responsibility in the direction of Gorazde and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their transfer from Serbia or rather Sandzak or rather the area of Raska -- and they were all militarily able-bodied Muslims, they were travelling towards Gorazde. The objective was for them to be engaged in combat. They were to be arrested so that they didn't reach Gorazde, and that was also to prevent possible sabotage activities in the rear. We were abreast of the intelligence about a possible destruction of the so-called blue bridge between Visegrad and Dobrun. Across Dobrun in the direction of Prijepolje, there were roads that they usually took. They skirted settled areas and they had very good reconnaissance of our units' positions. This is no news what I've just told you, and that is that Bosniaks from Sandzak were on the side of Bosniaks in Gorazde and elsewhere. I can also tell that you the former commander of the BiH army also hails from Sandzak, so this is no big secret at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to move to my second-to-last topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- one further question. Do I understand from your answer that those who travelled there, coming from Sandzak, were militarily able-body Muslims and that they wanted to become members of the armed forces at the end of their journey. Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, just -- they were still civilians if they are not yet members of the armed forces and if they are just able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, those travelling from Sandzak towards Gorazde. However, we had information and we had an order to take prisoners among those who had already joined the BiH army on the front line. And that order covered also the capture of unit members on the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's all fine. But those who were travelling, you said it had nothing to do with civilians. But they were not members of the armed forces. They may have wanted to become members of the armed forces; but they were not yet, if I well understood your testimony, and I sought verification of your initial answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not travel individually. First, they gathered in collection centres. They were equipped in a certain sense there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Equipped with what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military equipment and weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, but earlier you said these were able-bodied men travelling there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wishing, perhaps, to become members of the armed forces but not yet being. Now, if I receive a weapon and if I get military equipment, then I'm not an able-bodied man anymore but -- well, doesn't change, of course, the physical condition. But then you are -- have become a soldier. Whereas in your previous answer, there was a strong suggestion that they were not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had received equipment and weapons already in Sandzak. They didn't travel to Sandzak with their hands empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those in the trains, they were travelling there with weapons and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I seek clarification for one of the last answers of the witness. Sir, you said: "They had received equipment and weapons already in Sandzak." And then the next sentence reads: "They didn't travel to Sandzak with their hands empty." Were they already equipped and did they have their weapons when they went to Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mistake. Not to Sandzak. To Gorazde. They didn't travel to Gorazde with their hands empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to return to the four ethnic Muslim villages in your zone of responsibility. You were shown only one part of your prior Popovic testimony by Mr. Weber at transcript page 33394 and onwards. I would like to show you another part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could 65 ter number 32312 in e-court. And we'll need page 44 of the same. And that should correlate to transcript page 29155 of the Popovic proceedings. And if we could zoom in on lines 1 through 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will have to read this for you so you can get a translation, sir. "Q. Were you aware, sir, that in the fall of 1994, Muslims were moved out of Satorovici and Serb civilians were moved in? Were you aware of that? "A. Yes. I know [sic] that they had been moved out, that they want to the move out, and that they moved out in an organised manner. I don't know when that was. It may have been at the time when I had already left for the General Staff -- rather, the Main Staff. I also know that when they expressed their wish to move out, this met with some resistance. In Sarajevo, they did not want to take them, there were certain problems, some delays and procrastination when it came to their transfer." Sir, do you stand by what is written here as being both accurate and truthful as related to your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to ask you: Does this refresh your recollection or can you tell us now when you talked about people perhaps leaving in 1994, was that in relation to all four villages or was it perhaps in relation to just one of the four villages, Satorovici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I have already told you that some of them had moved out in 1994 based on what I knew, and you will find that in my statement. The rest of the population moved out towards the end of 1995, after the Dayton Accords. The fact is that some moved out in 1994, whereas the rest of the population moved out from the other villages towards the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move to my final topic, modified air bombs. You gave some information during cross-examination about the testing of the modified air bombs. I want to first ask you: What is the source of your information as to the development and testing of modified air bombs? How did you come to that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the development and testing of modified air bombs in the territory of Republika Srpska from my predecessors, Colonel Rajko Balac, and an engineer -- or rather, engineers from Pretis holding who were involved in the modification and development of those air bombs. Based on their explanations, I know - not directly that they had co-operated with certain experts in the Army of Yugoslavia. In addition to that, I've already mentioned that when I personally got acquainted with all that and when I prepared crews to man those tools, I saw the original firing tables that could only be compiled after a certain piece of equipment is tested and measured for ballistics, metrologic weight, and other parameters that are encompassed by the testing of every artillery system.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If can we call up P7245. This is a document that you were shown during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Ivetic, you're not completely happy with the -- yes, now it -- there was a transcript where you were transformed into Mr. Tieger but it has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for showing me that. I did -- I actually missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document that you were shown by the Prosecution talks of ground-to-ground missiles exploding near the city centre and it talks of the missiles deploying parachutes during their terminal descent. Did the modified air bombs as used by the Army of Republika Srpska utilise parachutes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The bombs were propelled by rocket engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the launchers that we had at the VRS, could multiple modified air bombs be launched simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Individually. Only individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you also tell us, you were asked by Mr. Weber about the lack of a barrel on the modified air bomb launchers. Now Grad rockets when they are launched from a multiple rocket-launcher - that is to say, in their original configuration without air bombs - how would you describe the inner surface of the barrel that launches a Grad rocket from a multiple-missile launcher system, Grad system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike a classical or conventional artillery tools, multiple-rocket launchers, both our own and foreign made, and Grad is Russian made, air bombs are fired from a smooth barrel. That barrel is open on both side, it had openings on both side, in the bag to release the gases from a rocket fuel and to push the rocket towards its goal. The rocket engine is active until midway and then it's shut off, and then the projectile travels by inertia to its target. The same principle is applied in air bomb, modified air bombs, but those bombs could not be placed in a barrel but rather on a launcher, and I've already explained how that looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said unlike classical or conventional artillery tools, the barrel is smooth, I think you said. Could you describe for us the difference between smooth barrels and the other type of barrels to begin with when it comes to artillery weapons. That will be my first question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barrels of conventional artillery tools have grooves at a certain angle all the way through the barrel. A projectile or a shell which is lodged in the back of such a barrel, when it is fired it is pushed by gun powder fumes that are created in the barrel. The projectile has a ring which is then pressed into the grooves and it rotates under a certain angle. That's how it gains stability on its trajectory to the target. This is for conventional tools. In rockets, air bombs, there is -- there are no grooves but a rocket engine gives it power to propel itself to the target. The principle is more or the less same minus the rotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And you also answered the additional question I anticipated to ask you. On behalf of the General Mladic and the rest of the team, I thank you for answering my questions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all have I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. I would have one question -- well, perhaps you listen carefully as well, Mr. Ivetic. You were asked about the use of parachutes. And you said no, they were not used, they were propelled by -- I don't know exactly, I think by the engines. Well, of course -- Unless, Mr. Ivetic, that's what you intended to ask the witness, whether there was any modified bomb that would be propelled by parachutes, I understood the report to say that in its flight that on from a certain point instead of just falling down that parachutes would open so as to slow down the speed of their descent. Therefore, I didn't understand the question to refer to anything propelling the -- propelling the projectile, but the answer did go in that direction, whereas I have difficulties in combining or to link your question and the answer given by the witness. If you could clarify that, that would certainly assist. And if the witness could tell us as well whether he is aware of the use of parachutes at all in any such projectiles, I would appreciate to receive an answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's take that into two parts. First of all, sir, the document indicates -- the document we have on our screen indicates that the missiles deployed parachutes during their terminal descent. Did the VRS modified air bombs utilize parachutes in the manner that is reflected in this document that we have before us whose number, unfortunately, escapes me, but I think it is P7245. Did the VRS modified air bombs utilize the parachutes in the manner that is described by this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor -- nor was it possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I guess we have to have two more questions. Could you first tell us why it was not possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply because we did not have any way to mount a parachute on a bomb so that it would be open at a given point in time. Further on, as a soldier I have to say that I don't know that any air bomb descends from an aircraft using a parachute. Probably it -- the wind would carry the parachute wherever rather than being part of a system either from land or air.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now the final question I have: Did the modified aerial bombs used by the VRS utilize parachutes at all in any manner, fashion, or capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA MASAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in any way. I am not aware of that even in theory, let alone in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that clarifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly clarifies a lot. Mr. Weber, any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
